title: Moses Asked God, “Who Am I?” God’s Answer Wasn’t About Moses
paragraphs: Moses Asked God, “Who Am I?” God’s Answer Wasn’t About Moses
The Call of Moses — and the terrifyingly beautiful truth that God’s answer to your inadequacy has never been your adequacy.
There is a question people usually ask when they are standing close to something bigger than themselves.
Not when life is comfortable.
Not when everything makes sense.
But when the assignment feels too heavy.
When the past feels too dirty.
When the responsibility feels too large.
When God seems to be calling you toward something your confidence cannot carry.
“Who am I?”
Moses asked it.
And maybe you have too.
Maybe not out loud.
Maybe yours sounded like:
“Why would God use someone like me?”
“After what I’ve done?”
“With my failures?”
“With my fear?”
“With this weakness I keep trying to hide?”
“I’m not spiritual enough.”
“I don’t know enough Scripture.”
“I’ve wasted too many years.”
“I’ve made too many mistakes.”
“I’m too ordinary.”
“I’m too broken.”
“Who am I?”
That question sounds humble.
Sometimes it is.
But hidden inside it can be a dangerous assumption:
That everything God is asking you to do ultimately depends on the answer.
And at a burning bush in the wilderness, God shattered that assumption.
Because when Moses asked, “Who am I?”
God did not spend the next few sentences explaining who Moses was.
He told Moses who would be with him.
And that changes everything.
Moses had not arrived at this moment as the triumphant prince of Egypt.
He was a shepherd.
A fugitive.
A man whose story already contained blood, failure, fear, rejection, and exile.
Exodus 2 tells us that Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Moses looked around, killed the Egyptian, and hid his body in the sand.
The next day, when Moses tried to intervene between two Hebrews, one of them answered with words that must have cut deeply:
“Who made you a prince and a judge over us?”
Then came the terrifying question:
“Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?”
Moses knew.
His secret was no longer secret.
Pharaoh heard about it and sought to kill him.
So Moses fled Egypt.
The man once raised in Pharaoh’s household disappeared into Midian and became a shepherd.
Then came the wilderness.
Years passed.
Egypt continued without him.
Israel continued suffering without him.
Whatever dreams Moses once carried seemed buried somewhere behind him.
And perhaps that is exactly why the burning bush matters so much.
God met Moses in a wilderness.
Not on a throne.
Not in Pharaoh’s palace.
Not while Moses looked impressive.
Not while Moses was building a reputation.
God came to him while he was tending somebody else’s sheep.
Then Moses saw something impossible.
A bush was burning…
but it was not being consumed.
He turned aside.
And God called his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
He answered:
“Here I am.”
Then God told him not to come closer.
“Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.”
This was not motivational speaking.
This was holiness.
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had drawn near.
Moses hid his face because he was afraid to look at God.
Then God said something Israel desperately needed to hear:
He had seen their affliction.
He had heard their cry.
He knew their sufferings.
And He had come down to deliver them.
But then the conversation turned.
God said, in essence:
Moses…
I am sending you.
Imagine what that sentence awakened inside him.
Egypt.
Pharaoh.
The murder.
The escape.
The rejection.
The years of obscurity.
The people who might remember.
The people who might ask questions.
The ruler who would not want to listen.
And Moses answered:
“Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?”
In Hebrew, the opening words are:
מִי אָנֹכִי — mi anokhi
“Who am I?”
It is one of the most painfully human questions in Scripture.
But watch God’s answer carefully.
God does not say:
“Moses, you need greater self-esteem.”
He does not say:
“Remember how talented you are.”
He does not give Moses a list of personality strengths.
He does not say:
“You were raised in Egypt, so believe in yourself.”
The Lord answers:
כִּי־אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ — ki ehyeh immakh
“But I will be with you.”
Exodus 3:12.
Moses asks about Moses.
God answers with God.
Read that again.
Moses asks:
“Who am I?”
God answers:
“I will be with you.”
Because the decisive issue was never whether Moses was impressive enough.
The decisive issue was whether God would be with him.
And perhaps this is where your own story begins to crack open.
You keep presenting God with your résumé.
God keeps presenting you with His presence.
You keep telling Him why you are insufficient.
He keeps reminding His people that His purposes do not rest upon human sufficiency.
You say:
“But Lord, look at me.”
And Scripture keeps turning your eyes away from yourself and back toward Him.
This does not mean your weakness is imaginary.
Moses really was afraid.
Moses really did struggle.
Moses really had a past.
Later he would object that he was not eloquent. He would question whether Israel would believe him. He would ask what he should say. Eventually he would plead for God to send someone else.
Scripture does not airbrush Moses into a fearless superhero.
That is exactly why his story is so powerful.
God’s answer to human weakness is not pretending weakness does not exist.
It is revealing that weakness does not have the final word when God is present.
There is an even deeper moment coming.
Moses asks what he should tell Israel when they ask for the name of the God who sent him.
God answers in Exodus 3:14:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה — Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh
Traditionally rendered:
“I AM WHO I AM.”

The Hebrew expression carries a depth that should make us cautious about reducing it to a slogan; translations such as “I AM WHO I AM” and “I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE” reflect the relationship of ehyeh to the Hebrew verb of being/becoming. In the immediate context, the same form ehyeh has already appeared in God’s promise to Moses:
“I will be with you.”
Moses is consumed with the question:
“Who am I?”
God progressively redirects the entire encounter toward the greater question:
Who is the God who sends him?
That is the question that changes everything.
Because Moses will not defeat Pharaoh through personality.
He will not divide the sea through charisma.
He will not bring Israel out because he finally discovers that deep inside himself he was powerful all along.
No.
The Exodus is designed to reveal the power, faithfulness, holiness, judgment, mercy, and covenant faithfulness of God.
Moses is the servant.
God is the Deliverer.
And Christians must go even further.
Because the Exodus does not end our story.
It prepares us to understand a greater rescue.
Centuries later, another Deliverer would come.
Not Moses.
Jesus Christ.
Moses was sent to confront Pharaoh and lead an enslaved people toward freedom.
Jesus came to accomplish the redemption Moses could never accomplish.
Moses was a servant in God’s house.
Christ is the Son.
Moses led Israel through the waters.
Christ brings sinners from death to life.
Moses mediated the old covenant.
Jesus is the Mediator of the new covenant.
And at the center of Christianity stands another scene that looked, from a human perspective, like scandal and defeat:
A cross.
The promised Messiah rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified between criminals.
His followers scattered.
His body placed in a tomb.
If you had looked only at Friday, you might have thought evil had won.
But Sunday was coming.
The stone would not remain the final punctuation mark.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
The cross became the place where sin was judged and grace was displayed.
The apparent scandal became the announcement of redemption.
And suddenly the pattern becomes impossible to miss.
God specializes in writing redemption where human beings see endings.
Moses had a wilderness.
Peter had a denial.
Paul had a history of persecuting the church.
The thief beside Jesus had a criminal’s cross and almost no time left.
Yet grace entered their stories.
That does not make sin unimportant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Biblical grace never says your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more than we want to admit.
Grace says something far more breathtaking:
Your sin is not greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
This is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for your past.
It is turning from sin toward the God who alone can save you from it.
You do not need to manufacture a cleaner history before coming to Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
The Gospel is not:
“Fix yourself until God can tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Jesus Christ for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Christ died for sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ was raised.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
And when you place your confidence in Christ rather than yourself, even the question “Who am I?” begins to lose its throne.
Because Christianity was never ultimately about discovering how extraordinary you are.
It is about discovering how glorious Christ is.
Maybe that is the sentence someone reading this has been running from.
You have spent years trying to become enough.
Enough for your parents.
Enough for your spouse.
Enough for the people who underestimated you.
Enough for the people who abandoned you.
Enough for church people.
Enough for yourself.
Maybe you even turned Christianity into another exhausting attempt to prove yourself.
Pray enough.
Serve enough.
Know enough.
Look holy enough.
Never let anyone discover the struggle.
Smile when somebody asks how you are doing.
Post the verse.
Hide the wound.
Lift your hands in worship while privately wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
And somewhere underneath all of it:
Who am I?
Listen to the burning bush again.
The answer is not found by staring harder at yourself.
“I will be with you.”
And for the Christian, that promise reaches an extraordinary fulfillment in Christ.
Before His ascension, Jesus commissioned His disciples to make disciples of all nations.
And He ended with a promise:
“And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.”
Matthew 28:20.
Do you see the beauty?
God’s people are given an impossible mission…
and the foundation is still not human greatness.
His presence.
“I will be with you.”
“I am with you always.”
This does not mean every dream you have is secretly a divine calling.
It does not mean believing hard enough guarantees success.
It does not mean Christians become invincible, wealthy, admired, or free from suffering.
Moses himself would endure opposition, frustration, grief, and consequences for his own disobedience.
Following God is not a promise of an easy life.
It is a summons to trust and obey the living God.
Sometimes obedience will cost you.
Sometimes it will lead straight through wilderness.
Sometimes faithfulness will make you misunderstood.
Sometimes God will expose idols you desperately wanted to keep.
Sometimes He will call you to forgive when bitterness feels safer.
Sometimes repentance will require admitting what you have spent years hiding.
Sometimes following Jesus will mean laying down the version of yourself you worked desperately to protect.
But you were never promised that following Christ would make the road painless.
You were promised something better than comfort.
Christ Himself.
Maybe your burning bush is not a literal miracle in the desert.
Maybe it is the moment Scripture finally confronts the thing you keep avoiding.
The apology you know you owe.
The secret sin you keep feeding.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The calling you keep postponing because you are terrified of failing.
The Gospel you are embarrassed to share.
The relationship pulling you away from Christ.
The private habit slowly hollowing out your soul.
The church community you abandoned because being known frightened you.
The prayer you stopped praying because disappointment taught you not to hope.
And perhaps your answer has been:
“God, You don’t understand who You’re dealing with.”
Oh, He does.
He knew Moses before Moses removed his sandals.
He knew about Egypt.
He knew about the body in the sand.
He knew about Midian.
He knew every objection Moses was about to make.
God did not discover Moses’ weakness halfway through the conversation.
And Jesus did not discover your history after calling sinners to Himself.
Nothing about your past surprises the One who calls you to repentance.
But do not twist grace into permission to remain unchanged.
The same grace that forgives also begins transforming.
Jesus does not rescue us so we can comfortably make peace with the chains He died to break.
Grace does not whisper:
“Stay exactly as you are forever.”
Grace calls:
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow.
Be changed.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to improve your self-image when He is trying to deepen your God-image.
Maybe you do not need another speech telling you that you are powerful.
Maybe you need to remember that He is.
Maybe you do not need to become the hero of your story.
Maybe you need to surrender to the Hero who entered history to save sinners.
Moses asked:
“Who am I?”
God’s answer was:
“I will be with you.”
And eventually Moses walked back toward the place he had fled.
Think about that.
The fugitive returned to Egypt.
The shepherd stood before Pharaoh.
The man filled with objections became an instrument through whom God displayed His power.
But never confuse the instrument with the Hand holding it.
Moses did not become God.
Moses remained Moses.
God remained God.
That was enough.
And perhaps that is freedom for you today.
You do not need to become somebody else before you can obey the next clear thing God has placed before you.
You do not need a spotless past to come to Jesus.
You do not need to pretend your weakness disappeared.
You need Christ.
You need grace.
You need repentance.
You need the Spirit of God.
You need Scripture.
You need the fellowship of believers.
You need to stop building an identity from wounds Jesus is calling you to surrender.
And if you have fallen…
come back.
If you have wandered…
come back.
If your prayer life has become almost silent…
come back.
If sin has made you ashamed to look toward heaven…
come back.
Not because sin is small.
Because Jesus is a mighty Savior.
Do not let shame preach a counterfeit gospel to you.
Shame says:
“Hide until you are worthy.”
Jesus calls sinners to come.
Shame says:
“Your worst chapter is your identity.”
The Gospel says redemption is found in Christ.
Shame says:
“You ruined everything.”
The cross says sin is deadly.
The resurrection says death itself did not get the final word.
That is not permission to romanticize failure.
It is the confession that Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing consequences.
He rewrites everything by bringing redemption into places sin tried to claim permanently.
Talk to Him.
Confess honestly.
Someone else may read your words tonight and realize they are not the only believer struggling to keep walking.
And if your spirit has been exhausted lately, there is no shame in simply writing:
“Pray for me.”
Let the body of Christ behave like the body of Christ.
Encourage somebody.
Point somebody toward Jesus.
Because this cannot end as merely another article you consumed.
Truth asks something from us.
If you know someone who keeps asking, “Who am I to do what God is asking me to do?” send this to them personally.
Not to advertise yourself.
Not to appear religious.
Your share could put the Gospel in front of someone who would never have searched for a sermon.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can itself be an act offered for God’s glory when it is done freely, wisely, and from a heart that wants Christ proclaimed. Salvation cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.
Because eventually every one of us reaches our own wilderness.
Every résumé becomes insufficient.
Every mask gets heavy.
Every human source of confidence eventually shakes.
And somewhere in that wilderness, the old question rises again:
“Who am I?”
When it does, remember the answer God gave Moses.
He did not inflate Moses.
He revealed Himself.
Your hope is not that one day you will finally become impressive enough to stop needing God.
Your hope is that in Jesus Christ you never have to.
The burning bush was never telling Moses how great Moses could become.
It was revealing how great the God who called him already was.
And maybe the sentence you need to carry with you after everything else fades is this:
Your past may explain why you tremble at the calling—but it does not get to sit on the throne where Christ belongs.
